title: Articles of Note: Week of July 20, 2026
author: Moore, Jason
summary: Jason Moore's weekly classical education roundup for the week of July 20, 2026 curates articles on classical education philosophy, liberal arts vs. vocational training, school discipline, calculus debates, writing instruction, and school choice. Featured authors include Christopher Perrin, Robert Pondiscio, Liz Cohen, Jackie Mader, Kate Bierly, and Anna Egalite, among others. The roundup reflects growing interest in the value and reach of classical education in both domestic and international contexts.
points: Christopher Perrin argues that true education means cultivating the full human being, not vocational training
Robert Pondiscio reviews The Science of Discipline, arguing schools need character formation, not just therapeutic empathy
John Mark N. Reynolds calls on classical education to stay rooted in the concerns of ordinary people
Karen Elliott asks what classical Christian education has to offer Africa, challenging assumptions about development needs
Madeleine Burr and Patrick Henry College argue that classical education produces the communication, integrity, and adaptability employers actually want
quotes: It ought not to be controversial to say that education is aimed at the cultivation and maturity of a human being.

Many of us are returning to the "classical" education that existed for more than a thousand years prior to the progressive revolution. What did we call classical education before 1890? Simply, education.
Anybody who still believes in the liberal arts believes that higher education exists for a higher purpose than putting graduates in jobs.

What in the world does classical Christian education have to do with Africa? What Africans really need is training in farming. All I see on the news are famines across Africa. They need to learn to feed themselves. In other words, why doesn't someone teach them how to fish instead of just giving them fish?
